meta.title: A town's first data center: what to require before saying yes
meta.subtitle: A requirements guide for local officials, planning boards, and residents facing a first data center proposal.

license.attribution: Community Goal — a town's first data center (github.com/caffeinated1/configurationRotBot), CC BY 4.0

meta.contributions: Open to anyone: residents, town staff, NGOs, agencies, and practitioners. Contributions are accepted under CC BY 4.0 for content and MIT for code, and contributors disclose any interest in a data center project. See GOVERNANCE.md.
meta.source_note: Content is a structured rendering of the source guide. Figures and case references are reproduced as stated in the source document; the source does not name its citations, so treat every figure as a claim to verify locally before relying on it in a hearing.
meta.disclaimer: This is not legal advice. Authority for zoning conditions, exactions, payments, and utility commitments varies by state. Confirm every item with counsel licensed in your jurisdiction.

goal.statement: Before the final vote, the town should be able to tell residents in plain language: what will be built, what it will consume, what the public receives, what happens if it fails, who enforces the agreement, and who pays to take it down.
goal.rule: If any of those answers is incomplete, resolve it before granting the approval that spends the last of the town's leverage.
goal.why_it_matters: A data center can bring construction employment, tax base, and infrastructure investment. It can also impose demands on electricity, water, public services, and nearby neighborhoods that last for decades and outlive the equipment inside.
goal.posture: No agreement prevents disputes from reaching court. The goal is to resolve routine problems in days, and to have money and legal authority already in place for the serious ones.

framing.heading: Two facts should frame everything

facts.claim: The industry produces very few permanent jobs relative to its cost.
facts.detail: One watchdog analysis of eleven major projects found subsidies averaging about $1.95 million per job.

facts.claim: Incentives are rarely what decides siting.
facts.detail: In a survey of data center owners, only three percent named tax credits and local incentives as the biggest siting factor. Land and power availability drive the decision.

framing.conclusion: You are usually not paying for something that would otherwise not happen.

basic_rule.statement: Every important promise needs a stated limit, a reliable way to check it, a responsible party with money behind it, and a practical response when it is broken.

pillars.name: Stated limit
pillars.question: Is the promise written as a number or an objective condition, not an intention?
pillars.failure_mode: A commitment phrased as 'will use best efforts to minimize' cannot be violated, so it cannot be enforced.

pillars.name: Reliable way to check it
pillars.question: Who measures it, with what equipment and method, how often, and is the raw data retained and published?
pillars.failure_mode: A limit the town cannot independently measure is a limit the applicant self-certifies.

pillars.name: Responsible party with money behind it
pillars.question: Who signs, and is that entity solvent, named, verified, and backed by security the town can reach?
pillars.failure_mode: A single-purpose project company with no assets can breach every term and pay nothing.

pillars.name: Practical response when it is broken
pillars.question: What happens in days, not years — and does the town keep every other lawful remedy?
pillars.failure_mode: A remedy that requires litigation to activate is not a remedy for a routine problem.

instruments.name: Zoning and overlay standards
instruments.purpose: Suitable locations, setbacks, height, buffers, general performance standards

instruments.name: Site approval or conditional use permit
Financial security instruments
instruments.purpose: Cash, escrow, or letters of credit for defined defaults and closure

instruments.name: Utility agreements and regulatory filings
instruments.purpose: Service, infrastructure cost allocation, reliability, customer exposure

final_questions.question: Who pays to take it down?
